Events, money and vendors at a glance.

Tasks still To do or Doing

text.text: Most events follow the same rhythm. Load these tasks when an event is booked and adjust the dates to its size.
Planning agreement signed and retainer paid
Budget agreed with the client, split by category
Venue booked; date held in writing
Caterer, photographer and music booked for large events
Save-the-dates for weddings and big galas
Rentals quoted: tables, chairs, linens, tent
Invitations ordered and sent (eight weeks for weddings)
Guest travel and room blocks set up if needed
Run of show drafted and shared with vendors
Insurance certificates collected from every vendor working at the venue
Final count to the caterer and venue by the
Vendor arrival times confirmed in writing
Emergency kit packed: tape, scissors, pins, stain remover, phone chargers, first aid

A corporate lunch for 24 needs a quarter of these steps over three weeks; a gala for 220 needs all of them over nine months. Delete the tasks that do not apply rather than leaving them open, so the overdue list stays honest. When a client books late, compress the timeline and tell them which choices will be limited.
Budget split, as a starting point
The Marchetti-Takahashi wedding is 75 days away. Invitations are going out late, so the team pushed the RSVP deadline back a week and moved the seating chart task to match.
A vendor booking is a contract and a payment schedule. Most day-of problems trace back to something not written down at booking.
Before you ask for a quote
Event date, venue, times, guest count and style
What you need exactly: number of pieces, staff, hours

cells.text: Must fit the client's payment schedule
What happens if the date moves
The venue will ask for a certificate
Past performance beats a low price

text.text: When the contract arrives, check names, date, times, inclusions and payments; set
Enter the deposit, its due date and the balance due date. Tick
Ask for the insurance certificate naming the venue; tick it when received.
After the event and final payment, set
Never sign on the client's behalf unless your agreement says you may.
Every change after signing is confirmed in writing, with the new price.
Vendors get one contact person from our side.
Meals and breaks for vendor staff are agreed in advance.
When a vendor misses a deposit date

If we miss a deposit, the vendor may release the date. Pay or call that day. If a vendor misses their own promise, such as a late contract, write down what was agreed and when, and tell the client before it becomes a problem on the day.
Rate the vendor and add a note. "Arrived late, great work" helps the next planner choose.

Saltwater Table's contract for the wedding has been sent, with a 6,300 dollar deposit due in six days. The client has the contract; the planner has a task to confirm signature before the deposit date.
The run of show is the minute-by-minute plan everyone works from on the day. A clear one means you can step away and the event keeps running.
Times for every moment: vendor arrivals, doors, speeches, dinner service, first dance, last call, end, load-out
Who does what at each moment, and who cues it
Contact numbers for every vendor lead
Work backwards from the guest arrival time.
Leave 15-minute buffers around speeches and dinner service.
Share a draft two weeks out; ask each vendor to confirm their lines.
Final version goes to everyone 48 hours before, with any changes highlighted.
Rain and other plan B moments

Every outdoor moment needs a written backup: where the ceremony moves, who decides and by when, and how chairs and decor move. Put the decision time in the run of show, such as 2 pm for a 5 pm ceremony, so nobody argues at 4:45.
One planner holds the run of show and the timing; another handles guests and surprises.
Changes are told to every vendor lead, not just one.
Keep notes of what ran late and why for the wrap-up.

For the Coastal Pines client dinner, the venue asks for load-out by 23:00, half an hour earlier than planned. The run of show moves dessert forward by 15 minutes and every vendor lead gets the new version.
The week after an event is when you protect your reputation and your margin. Close every money item, thank everyone, and write down what you learned.
Rentals counted back; damage noted with photos
Gifts, decor and leftover items delivered where the client wants them
Every vendor's final invoice checked against the contract; overtime or extras confirmed.
Balances paid; each booking set to
Final budget report to the client: budget, committed costs, extras, and why.

cells.text: The cause and the fix next time
A rating and a note on their booking
Where the next budget should change

text.text: Compare the final budget with the first one. Extras the client approved belong in the report with the date they approved them. Our planning fee balance is invoiced the same week, while the client is still happy, with a short thank-you note on top.
Send a short note a week after with a link where they can leave a review, and ask whether you may use photos. Couples and companies often say yes when asked soon after.
Corporate clients: book the next date while the event is fresh.
Families and couples: note anniversaries and milestones for a friendly message next year.
Nonprofits: offer a debrief before they plan next year's gala.

The Pelham product summit wrapped 45 days ago. The caterer's final invoice matched the contract, sponsors were thanked, and Pelham has asked for dates for next year's summit, so a new inquiry is on the board.
Planners juggle dozens of dates, contracts and people for each event. This workspace keeps one record per event, with every vendor booking and task linked to it, so nothing depends on memory.
